nameStory: This fungus gets its scientific name 'aurantiaca' from the Latin word for orange, referring to its bright orange-red coloration that really pops against dark wood. While it doesn't have a widely-used common name, mycologists sometimes call it the 'orange jelly crust' for its distinctive gelatinous, pustule-like appearance that looks almost like tiny orange blisters on wood.
description: Orange jelly crust is a peculiar fungus that doesn't look like your typical mushroom at all. Instead of caps and stems, it forms small, bright orange-red blobs that look like gelatinous pustules or tiny orange bubbles scattered across dead wood. These squishy, jelly-like growths are usually only a few millimeters across but can cluster together in patches. It's what mycologists call an 'anamorphic' fungus, meaning it reproduces without forming the familiar mushroom structures we typically think of.

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Brilliant orange to orange-red coloration that's hard to miss against dark wood backgrounds

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Gelatinous and squishy to the touch, like firm jelly or a soft gummy candy that bounces back when poked

idTips.label: Shape
idTips.description: Forms small pustule-like bumps or blister-shaped growths, often clustered together in patches

idTips.label: Substrate
idTips.description: Always found growing directly on dead deciduous wood, never on conifers or soil

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Individual pustules are tiny, typically just a few millimeters across, but colonies can spread over several inches of wood surface

habitat: Look for this distinctive fungus on dead branches, fallen logs, and decaying wood of deciduous trees throughout New England's forests. It's particularly fond of hardwood species like oak, maple, and birch, where it grows as a decomposer breaking down the dead wood. You'll spot it in both deep woods and forest edges, from lowland areas up into the mountains.

seasonality.spring: Fresh growths begin appearing on wood as moisture returns and temperatures warm. The bright orange color is most vibrant during this season.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season when the gelatinous pustules are most abundant and easiest to spot. Look after periods of rain when the wood stays moist.
seasonality.fall: Still actively growing and quite visible, though some older growths may start to fade or dry out as conditions become more variable.
seasonality.winter: May persist in dried form on wood, appearing more shriveled and less gelatinous, but can rehydrate during warm, wet spells.

funFact: This tiny fungus plays a crucial role as a mycorrhizal partner with orchids, helping these delicate flowers survive by providing essential nutrients - quite a career change from its day job of decomposing dead wood!
confusionNotes: The bright orange jelly-like texture makes this species quite distinctive, though it might be confused with other orange gelatinous fungi like orange witches' butter. However, those species typically grow in different, more bracket-like forms, while orange jelly crust always appears as small, separate pustules directly on wood surfaces.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its small size and unusual appearance, this fungus represents an important ecological bridge - it's one of the few species that can switch between being a wood decomposer and forming beneficial partnerships with plant roots, showcasing the amazing adaptability of fungal life.
compareHints: Orange jelly crust differs from its close relative Tulasnella violea primarily in color - while this species is bright orange-red, T. violea appears in purple to violet hues. Both share the same gelatinous, pustular growth form and preference for dead deciduous wood, but the dramatic color difference makes them easy to distinguish in the field.
